title: An A.I. school with no teachers heads for London. Britain’s private schools should worry. 2026
author: David James
source: Schools of Thought (drdavidajames.substack.com), first published in UnHerd, November 14,
summary: After visiting Alpha School in Austin, Texas, James examines what the AI-led school group's planned London opening means for Britain's already fragile independent sector. Alpha's founding claim is that children using adaptive software for two hours each morning, and not moving on until they show 90% mastery, learn twice as fast; adults act as paid 'guides' who coach and motivate rather than teach. He notes critics' point that results rest on the school's own testing of a self-selecting affluent intake, and observes gaps in the arts, humanities, sport and science practicals. Yet British independent schools, some closing after VAT reform, are vulnerable to a disruptive entrant. His broader concern is that AI will divide rather than level up, with the affluent getting both software and people and everyone else getting a screen. He argues AI should supplement teachers rather than replace them, that good tools should be free and independently evaluated, and that Alpha, which spends lavishly on people, may have more to teach British schools than critics allow.
points: Alpha's model rests on two hours of adaptive AI instruction each morning with a 90% mastery gate, with high-paid guides rather than conventional teachers, and a claim of learning at twice the pace.
James flags the evidence problem: the headline results come from Alpha's own testing of a self-selecting affluent intake, and pupils who struggle with the model tend to leave.
Even in showcase schools the creative arts, humanities and sport are outsourced or pared back and there are no science practicals, which raises questions about university readiness.
The London opening arrives when independent schools are vulnerable after VAT reform, making a low-teacher, high-tech rival a real threat.
His policy conclusion is that AI should supplement not replace teachers, with free tools judged on independent evidence, so that technology does not split the affluent from everyone else.
quotes: That is because Alpha schools have no teachers in the conventional sense and, as if that were not controversial enough, they unapologetically put artificial intelligence at the centre of their pupils’ learning.

The founding claim is that a child working with adaptive software for two hours a morning, and not allowed to move on until they have shown 90% mastery, learns at least twice as fast as a child in a traditional classroom.
Critics argue that Alpha’s impressive results rest largely on its own testing of a self-selecting, affluent intake, and that pupils who struggle with the model tend to leave.

Progress is checked not by teachers but by “guides”, who are paid around $100,000 a year — so as to attract high-calibre applicants — and recruited for their interpersonal skills rather than their subject knowledge.
But the real sanction is choice. Families sign up to Alpha’s ethos before they join, and high school pupils must opt in; those for whom the model repeatedly fails tend to move on.
AI can do many brilliant things, but it can’t capture the wonder of a dissection, or the moment a titration finally turns pink.

The danger is that this technology will divide rather than level up: the affluent will get both the innovative software and the people around it, while everyone else will get a screen to make up for the teachers the school cannot recruit.
If the benefits are to be spread widely, AI has to be treated as a supplement to teachers, not a replacement. Good tools should be free in schools, and judged on independent evidence.
context: The article's frame is that Alpha's no-teacher, AI-centred design is what makes it controversial.
The core claim of the model is mastery-gated adaptive software producing doubled learning speed.
James immediately weighs the claim against the self-selection critique.
Guides are hired for relationships and paid well, which shifts the adult role from instruction to motivation.
Retention by choice rather than sanction shapes how Alpha's results should be read.
A concrete example of what an AI-led curriculum cannot replace.
His central worry is that AI deepens inequality between schools rather than closing gaps.
His policy conclusion is that AI should supplement teachers and be independently evaluated.
